title: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition) · Units 29–30
description: Natural English expressions for preparing and giving presentations, communicating data, recruitment, career development and everyday work.

units.title: Unit 29 — Presentations
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 62–63 (PDF pages 66–67).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Work and study · presentations and public speaking
learningObjectives: Prepare and deliver presentations with accurate verb–noun combinations and a clear central message.
Speak to a target audience using natural expressions for eye contact, gesture, voice and handling questions.
Describe visual aids, slides, diagrams and data with correct terminology and collocations.
Avoid typical learner errors in expressions involving impact, slide readability, charts and key points.

items.example: I need to prepare a presentation for Friday's engineering meeting.
items.note: Prepare means organise the content and materials before speaking; do a presentation is possible informally but give a presentation is the usual delivery verb.

items.pt: fazer uma apresentação; apresentar uma palestra
items.example: Our manager will give a presentation about the new project.
items.note: Give is the conventional verb for delivering a presentation to an audience.

items.word: a structure that is easy to follow
items.example: A structure that is easy to follow helps listeners understand each stage of a talk.
items.note: Easy to follow describes a clear logical organisation, rather than how large the text appears on a slide.

items.example: Use one clear diagram to communicate your core message.
items.note: Your core message is the central idea you want listeners to remember.

items.pt: uma mensagem central; a ideia principal
items.example: A core message should be clear even to people outside the project.
items.note: Core means central or most important, not merely a short message.

items.example: The target audience includes engineers and laboratory technicians.
items.note: The target audience is the specific group that the content is intended to reach.

items.example: A clear example can hold the audience's attention better than a long list of figures.
items.note: Hold someone's attention means keep them interested and focused; keep is also possible.

items.example: Short demonstrations can keep their attention during a long workshop.
items.note: Keep someone's attention describes maintaining interest over time.

items.example: An interactive presentation gives participants opportunities to ask questions.
items.note: Interactive means the listeners participate, rather than only watch and listen.

items.pt: criar conexão com o público; estabelecer contato com a plateia
items.example: Simple questions can help you connect with your audience.
items.note: Connect with means establish rapport and make communication feel relevant to listeners.

items.example: Your body language can reinforce your message before you speak.
items.note: Body language includes posture, movement and gestures, not just facial expression.

items.pt: ficar em pé com a postura ereta
items.example: Try to stand up straight when you address a large audience.
items.note: Stand up straight is a common physical instruction about posture; sitting up straight is the seated alternative.

items.example: Natural hand gestures can help explain the size of a component.
items.note: Hand gestures are movements made with the hands; very large or frequent gestures may distract listeners.

items.pt: enfatizar seu argumento; destacar seu ponto
items.example: You can emphasise your point by repeating the main result once.
items.note: Emphasise is standard British spelling; emphasize is an American variant.

items.example: Try to make eye contact with different people in the room.
items.note: Make eye contact means look directly at another person's eyes briefly when communicating.

items.example: It is uncomfortable to maintain eye contact with one listener for the whole talk.
items.note: Maintain suggests continuing eye contact, not only making it once.

items.example: Before speaking, breathe deeply to help yourself relax.
items.note: Deeply is the natural adverb with breathe in this calming instruction.

items.example: Speak clearly when you introduce unfamiliar technical terms.
items.note: Clearly refers to being easy to understand, including pronunciation and articulation.

items.example: A calm tone of voice can make complex information easier to follow.
items.note: Tone of voice conveys a speaker's manner and emotion; it is not only loudness.

items.example: Public speaking becomes easier with regular practice.
items.note: A noun phrase naming the activity or skill of addressing an audience.

items.pt: lidar com perguntas; responder a questionamentos
items.example: Allow enough time to deal with questions at the end of the presentation.
items.note: Deal with questions means address them appropriately, not necessarily know every answer.

items.example: Listen carefully before trying to answer a difficult question.
items.note: Carefully signals close attention rather than casual hearing.

items.example: We should prepare handouts for participants who need the circuit diagrams.
items.note: Handouts are materials distributed to an audience; prepare them before the session.

items.example: The organiser will give out handouts after the training session.
items.note: Give out means distribute to several people; hand out is an alternative verb.

items.pt: recursos visuais; materiais de apoio visual
items.example: Visual aids such as charts and photographs can clarify an explanation.
items.note: Visual aids are images, diagrams, videos or other materials that help an audience understand.

items.pt: recursos visuais claros e fáceis de entender
items.example: Use clear visual aids when presenting the test results.
items.note: Clear describes legibility and ease of interpretation, not just image resolution.

items.example: A simple live demonstration can make an impact on the audience.
items.note: Make an impact on someone means produce a noticeable or strong effect.

items.example: A well-designed chart can have an impact on how people understand the findings.
items.note: Have an impact on is another natural collocation; give an impact is not standard.

items.example: An effective presentation answers the audience's most important questions.
items.note: Effective means successful in achieving the intended communication goal.

items.example: We used presentation software to organise the slides.
items.note: The phrase describes applications designed for creating and displaying presentations.

items.example: Keep slides simple so the audience can focus on your explanation.
items.note: Keep something simple is a verb–adjective pattern, not keep it simply.

items.example: Choose a clear font for labels on your diagrams.
items.note: A clear font is easy to read; font refers to the style of lettering.

items.example: Make sure the text on every slide is easy to read.
items.note: Easy to read is the normal description for legible text, not easy to watch.

items.example: Write the key points on the board before showing the results.
items.note: Key identifies the most important ideas; big points is not the usual expression here.

items.example: The final slide should summarise the key issues for the team.
items.note: Key also naturally modifies issues, areas, elements and questions.

items.example: We will discuss the key questions after the demonstration.
items.note: Key questions are the most important questions that need answers.

items.pt: tópicos com marcadores; itens em lista
items.example: Bullet points are useful for showing three short recommendations.
items.note: The visual list items are bullet points, not full paragraphs.

items.pt: acompanhar seu raciocínio; entender sua argumentação
items.example: Explain each assumption so the audience can follow your argument.
items.note: Follow an argument means understand the reasoning as it develops; take an argument is not idiomatic here.

items.pt: um gráfico de pizza; gráfico de setores
items.example: A pie chart can show how a budget is divided into categories.
items.note: Pie charts display parts of a whole; they are not called cake charts.

items.example: A bar chart makes it easier to compare results across five systems.
items.note: Bar chart is the standard term, not bar table.

items.example: Use an appropriate chart to present data accurately.
items.note: Present data means communicate results, commonly through a chart, table or talk.

items.pt: tornar a apresentação mais interessante e dinâmica
items.example: Short animations can bring the presentation to life.
items.note: Bring something to life means make it feel vivid or engaging; carry something to life is not idiomatic.

items.example: Repeat your key points briefly when you reach the conclusion.
items.note: Repeat key points helps reinforce meaning; it does not imply repeating every slide.

items.pt: mostrar números ou dados com clareza
items.example: Use large labels to show figures clearly in your charts.
items.note: Figures here are numerical data, not illustrations of people.

items.word: use a lot of visual aids
items.example: You may use a lot of visual aids, but each one should support your explanation.
items.note: This phrase occurs in the exercise context; quantity alone does not make a presentation effective.

units.title: Unit 30 — Work
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 64–65 (PDF pages 68–69).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Work and study · career, recruitment and workplace tasks
learningObjectives: Distinguish job, work and career in natural combinations about employment and professional development.
Use appropriate collocations for vacancy advertisements, qualifications, benefits and teamworking.
Discuss workplace tasks, meetings, telephone calls, targets and resignation with accurate verb–noun patterns.
Describe career progression and contrast fulfilling, rewarding and lucrative employment.

items.example: I have a job in a research laboratory.
items.note: Say have a job when referring to employment; have a work is incorrect in this meaning.

items.example: Designing safety-critical software can be a demanding job.
items.note: Demanding means requiring substantial effort, ability or attention.

items.pt: um trabalho gratificante; um emprego realizador
items.example: Teaching can be a fulfilling job when you enjoy helping others learn.
items.note: Fulfilling describes personal satisfaction rather than high pay.

items.pt: um cargo de grande responsabilidade; um emprego de alto nível
items.example: She accepted a high-powered job at an international company.
items.note: High-powered suggests influence, status or major responsibilities; it does not describe electrical power.

items.example: After years of temporary contracts, he found a steady job.
items.note: Steady describes reliable, continuing employment.

items.example: He hopes to find a permanent job after his internship.
items.note: Permanent contrasts with temporary or fixed-term employment.

items.pt: candidatar-se a uma vaga de emprego
items.example: She plans to apply for a job in embedded software.
items.note: Apply for is the required preposition when requesting employment.

items.example: The company will offer someone a job after the final interview.
items.note: Offer someone a job has a person as its first object; offer a job to someone is also possible.

items.example: Our team will carry out work on the control system this week.
items.note: Carry out work refers to performing assigned activities or tasks.

items.example: An experienced technician will supervise work in the test area.
items.note: Supervise involves overseeing the work or its quality.

items.example: We need to complete work on the prototype before the review.
items.note: Complete means finish; work is generally uncountable in this sense.

items.example: Firmware developers often work closely with hardware designers.
items.note: Closely means in close cooperation; the preposition with names the collaborators.

items.example: The team cannot take on work outside the agreed scope this month.
items.note: Take on means accept responsibility for additional work.

items.example: The new engineer is expected to start work on Monday.
items.note: Start work refers to beginning work or a job, commonly without an article.

items.pt: estar disponível para começar a trabalhar
items.example: I will be available to start work after my current contract ends.
items.note: A common recruitment pattern for stating when a candidate can begin.

items.example: She wants to embark on a career in product development.
items.note: Embark on is relatively formal and means begin an important new activity or career.

items.pt: seguir carreira em engenharia; ter uma carreira na engenharia
items.example: Many graduates hope to have a career in engineering.
items.note: Have a career in introduces a professional field; career does not mean a single job.

items.example: He had a brilliant career in scientific research.
items.note: Brilliant suggests outstanding professional success or achievement.

items.example: The young designer has a promising career ahead of her.
items.note: Promising suggests likely future success, not necessarily current seniority.

items.pt: uma carreira decola; uma carreira deslancha
items.example: A career takes off when new opportunities lead to rapid progress.
items.note: Take off is an idiomatic phrasal verb for becoming successful quickly.

items.word: at the peak of your career
items.example: At the peak of your career, you may have many responsibilities.
items.note: Peak and height are natural alternatives indicating the most successful stage.

items.word: at the height of your career
items.example: You can still learn new skills at the height of your career.
items.note: At the height of describes the stage of greatest professional prominence.

items.example: She took management training to climb the career ladder.
items.note: A figurative expression for moving into positions of increasing seniority.

items.example: A serious ethical violation can ruin a career.
items.note: Ruin a career describes severe damage to someone's professional future; wreck is an emphatic alternative.

items.example: He had a long career in industrial automation.
items.note: Career describes a professional history or path over time; it differs from one specific job.

items.pt: ter bom conhecimento de; conhecer bem
items.example: Applicants should have a good knowledge of industrial communication protocols.
items.note: The pattern has have a good knowledge of followed by a field or topic.

items.pt: ter experiência na área de vendas
items.example: Candidates must have experience in sales and customer support.
items.note: Experience in introduces a field of work; experience with can introduce particular tools or tasks.

items.pt: alguém que trabalha bem em equipe
items.example: A good team player shares information and supports colleagues.
items.note: A team player collaborates effectively with other people.

items.example: A stimulating working environment encourages people to develop new skills.
items.note: Stimulating describes work conditions that are interesting and motivating.

items.pt: parte essencial de; componente integrante de
items.example: Testing is an integral part of product development.
items.note: An integral part of means a necessary or important component of a whole.

items.example: She enjoys working in a close team where people exchange ideas.
items.note: A close team consists of colleagues who work well together; close-knit team is also common.

items.example: Flexible schedules and meaningful tasks can improve job satisfaction.
items.note: Job satisfaction is how pleased someone feels with their job, not their salary alone.

items.pt: benefícios atrativos; pacote generoso de benefícios
items.example: The vacancy includes generous benefits and paid training.
items.note: Benefits are non-salary advantages; generous means more favourable than usual.

items.example: The department hopes to fill a vacancy before December.
items.note: Fill is the usual verb for hiring a person into an open position.

items.pt: assumir a responsabilidade por; ficar encarregado de
items.section: C · Things you might do at work
items.example: The new coordinator will take charge of the equipment inventory.
items.note: Take charge of means become responsible for managing or overseeing something.

items.section: C · Things you might do at work
items.example: We will test the configuration to make sure nothing goes wrong during the demonstration.
items.note: Make sure that expresses checking or arranging to prevent a problem.

items.section: C · Things you might do at work
items.example: The assistant will make appointments with clients next week.
items.note: Make an appointment means arrange a meeting or scheduled visit.

items.section: C · Things you might do at work
items.example: You should keep your appointments or tell people when you must cancel.
items.note: Keep an appointment means attend or honour it as agreed; make one means arrange it.

items.section: C · Things you might do at work
items.example: The receptionist will answer the phone while we are in the meeting.
items.note: Answer the phone is the normal phrase for responding when it rings.

items.section: C · Things you might do at work
items.example: A colleague will field telephone calls while the manager is travelling.
items.note: Field calls means handle them, answering or directing them as necessary.

items.section: C · Things you might do at work
items.example: We need to make reservations for the visiting research team.
items.note: Make is the standard verb for organising bookings; reserve also works as a verb.

items.section: C · Things you might do at work
items.example: We must make preparations before the annual equipment inspection.
items.note: Make preparations means arrange what is necessary in advance, not just plan mentally.

items.section: C · Things you might do at work
items.example: Please make photocopies of the safety checklist for the trainees.
items.note: Make photocopies means reproduce paper documents using a photocopier.

items.section: C · Things you might do at work
items.example: The office assistant will arrange meetings with the project partners.
items.note: Arrange means coordinate the time and details, not lead the meeting.

items.section: C · Things you might do at work
items.example: I will take the minutes during tomorrow's design review.
items.note: Minutes are the official written record of a meeting; take the minutes means prepare that record.

items.section: C · Things you might do at work
items.example: Technicians keep a record of each maintenance operation.
items.note: Keep a record of means document and preserve information for later reference.

items.section: C · Things you might do at work
items.example: To improve your speaking, set yourself targets for each month.
items.note: Set targets means establish measurable objectives; set yourself targets makes them personal goals.

items.pt: dar o seu melhor; fazer o máximo possível
items.section: C · Things you might do at work
items.example: Do your best to explain the problem without using unnecessary jargon.
items.note: Do your best means make the greatest reasonable effort; make your best is incorrect.

items.pt: atingir suas metas; alcançar seus objetivos
items.section: C · Things you might do at work
items.example: A clear study plan can help you achieve your goals.
items.note: Achieve combines naturally with goals, aims and objectives.

items.section: C · Things you might do at work
items.example: Before the project review, make a list of unresolved issues.
items.note: Use make a list, not do a list, when creating one.

items.pt: apresentar aviso de demissão; comunicar formalmente a saída do emprego
items.section: C · Things you might do at work
items.example: If you plan to change companies, you may need to hand in your notice.
items.note: Primarily British English; it means inform an employer formally that you are resigning.

items.section: C · Things you might do at work
items.example: He decided to take early retirement after thirty years at the company.
items.note: Early retirement means retiring before the standard or expected age.

items.section: D · Exercise-based career and recruitment language
items.example: The employer is looking for candidates with relevant qualifications.
items.note: Relevant qualifications are credentials related to the position being offered.

items.section: D · Exercise-based career and recruitment language
items.example: The vacancy advertises a competitive salary and flexible working hours.
items.note: Competitive means attractive relative to similar roles; it does not identify an exact amount.

items.pt: começar a trabalhar com pouca antecedência
items.section: D · Exercise-based career and recruitment language
items.example: The successful candidate must be able to start work at short notice.
items.note: At short notice means after little advance warning or preparation.

items.section: D · Exercise-based career and recruitment language
items.example: We need to meet deadlines without reducing the quality of our tests.
items.note: Meet is the natural verb with deadlines; miss a deadline is the opposite.

items.pt: trabalhar sob pressão; trabalhar em condições de estresse
items.section: D · Exercise-based career and recruitment language
items.example: She can work under stress during busy production periods.
items.note: Work under pressure is a more common alternative, but the exercise also uses under stress.

items.section: D · Exercise-based career and recruitment language
items.example: The contract specifies a period of notice before resignation.
items.note: A period of notice is the time between notifying an employer and leaving a job.

items.pt: um emprego sem perspectivas de crescimento
items.section: D · Exercise-based career and recruitment language
items.example: He left a dead-end job to train as an electrician.
items.note: A dead-end job offers little opportunity for progress or development.

items.pt: uma carreira brilhante e de grande destaque
items.section: D · Exercise-based career and recruitment language
items.example: The researcher enjoyed a glittering career in international science.
items.note: Glittering is figurative and stresses outstanding achievements or public admiration.

items.pt: uma carreira que se estende por cinco décadas
items.section: D · Exercise-based career and recruitment language
items.example: The documentary celebrates a career spanning five decades.
items.note: Spanning refers to the length of a career; another time period can follow.

items.pt: um emprego lucrativo; um trabalho muito bem remunerado
items.section: D · Exercise-based career and recruitment language
items.example: She accepted a lucrative job in financial consulting.
items.note: Lucrative emphasises financial rewards rather than personal fulfilment.

items.section: D · Exercise-based career and recruitment language
items.example: Supporting students can be a rewarding job.
items.note: Rewarding usually suggests emotional or personal satisfaction, not necessarily high income.

items.section: D · Exercise-based career and recruitment language
items.example: He wants a satisfying job where he can see the results of his work.
items.note: Satisfying is close to fulfilling and rewarding, but not necessarily financially lucrative.
